# Eric Yim — Organization Design Strategist

> Eric Yim is an organization design strategist specializing in human-AI work
> partnership — designing how organizations divide work between people and
> machines, and the structures, capabilities and behaviors that make that
> partnership work.

## What this site covers

The personal site of Eric Yim: what he believes about organizations, how he
works, and the playbook and diagnostic he uses. All sections are on one page:

- [How I think](https://www.ericyim.sg/#principles) — six principles behind
  the work.
- [How I work](https://www.ericyim.sg/#approach) — a six-stage method (Frame,
  Focus, Find, Dial, Design, Deliver) and three evidence grades.
- [Required, chosen or inherited?](https://www.ericyim.sg/#differences) — a
  lens for deciding what to do about differences between markets, sites or
  acquired units, with a two-question sorter.
- [The playbook](https://www.ericyim.sg/#playbook) — four tools:
  - [The framework](https://www.ericyim.sg/#framework) — Integrated
    Organizational Capability and Change Framework: four interdependent
    domains around a leadership core.
  - [The five activators](https://www.ericyim.sg/#activators) — what turns an
    organisation design into performance.
  - [The change model](https://www.ericyim.sg/#change-levers) — Communicate,
    Co-create, Cadence, plus the T.C.C.A.R. team-health lens.
  - [AI-native design](https://www.ericyim.sg/#ai-native) — descend to the
    task, place every task on an L0–L3 ladder, gate every machine judgement.
- [The diagnostic](https://www.ericyim.sg/#diagnostic) — an 18-question
  organisational health assessment scored across five dimensions.
- [About](https://www.ericyim.sg/#about) — entity, background and common
  questions.

## Biography

Eric Yim has spent 25 years in the gap between diagnosing an organization and
redesigning it. He graduated from Nanyang Technological University in 1998
specializing in financial analysis, began in corporate banking, and moved into
organizational development through the public sector — an unusual route that
gave him a systems view of organizations. He has since led organization
development and effectiveness work at L'Oréal, Shell and Cargill across
Asia-Pacific, EMEA and the Middle East, and is now Global Head of OD and
Talent at SATS Ltd. in Singapore, working at the intersection of
organizational development and AI adoption in the workplace. His talent work
at SATS was recognised with Gold for Talent Management & Acquisition at the
SHRI Singapore HR Awards 2025.

## Principles

Every diagnosis, design and plan on this site is built on these. Each one
links to the part of the playbook that puts it to work.

01. **A system, not a report.** A diagnosis is only worth what it hands leaders next: the decision, the
    owner and the first move. The work ends in a plan that runs, not a deck
    that sits.
02. **One system, not four fixes.** Structure, people, process and mindset move together, held by leadership,
    or they don’t move at all. A new chart on its own is a reorganization, not
    a redesign.
03. **Not every difference is a problem.** When two parts of a business work differently, ask why before you
    harmonise. Some differences are required, some were chosen and some were
    simply inherited, and each calls for a different decision.
04. **Change is a behaviour, not an announcement.** People usually know the why. What’s missing is the specific move each
    leader makes, the moment that makes it stick and the rhythm that keeps it
    going.
05. **AI redesigns the work, not the chart.** Go down to the task. Decide what is automated, assisted or kept human, and
    let a person, not a model, make the final call.
06. **Say what you know, and how you know it.** Separate what is confirmed from what is indicated and what is still a
    hypothesis. A gap marked “not scored” is honest; a guessed score becomes a
    false finding.

## How Eric Yim works

Every engagement follows the same arc. The first three stages establish what
is actually true. The last three decide what to change, install it, and prove
it worked.

- **Stage 0 — Frame.** What are we building, and how will we judge the design? Produces: agreed
  criteria, locked before the debate starts.
- **Stage 1 — Focus.** Where must the model change, and where does it matter most? Produces: a
  shortlist of where capability is weak where the value is made.
- **Stage 2 — Find.** How does the work really run, and who really decides? Produces:
  evidence-traced maps of paper versus practice.
- **Stage 3 — Dial.** What should be one way everywhere, and how much should AI do? Produces: a
  call on every difference and every task.
- **Stage 4 — Design.** Which structure, roles and system do we install together? Produces: options
  scored against the criteria from stage 0.
- **Stage 5 — Deliver.** Is it lifting capability, cycle by cycle? Produces: a scoreboard that holds
  each forecast to account.

Stage 0 is deliberate: agree how the design will be judged before anyone
argues for one.

Every finding carries one of three grades, and the grade sets what it can be
used for.

- **Confirmed** — Verified at source. Use it to: decide.
- **Indicated** — Supported, not yet verified. Use it to: decide with care, and say so.
- **Hypothesis** — Still to test. Use it to: never decide on this alone.

“Not scored” is a valid answer. A blank says we don’t know yet; a guess says
something false with confidence.

## Required, chosen and inherited differences

As a business grows across markets, sites and acquisitions, the same work ends
up done in different ways. Before harmonising anything, ask why each
difference exists. The answer tells you what to do.

- **Required** — Regulation, a customer contract or the physical site makes it so. Response:
  leave it local.
- **Chosen** — A deliberate local decision, made for a reason someone can still state.
  Response: decide: keep or align.
- **Inherited** — History, an acquisition or habit. Nobody decided it. Response: harmonise.

Two questions sort any difference: is it required by regulation, a customer
contract or the physical site; and if not, did someone decide it on purpose,
for a reason they can still state today?

## Answers

### Who is Eric Yim?

Eric Yim is an organization design strategist specializing in human-AI work
partnership. He has spent 25 years working between organizational diagnosis
and redesign, and works at the intersection of organizational development and
AI adoption in the workplace.

### What is human-AI work partnership?

Human-AI work partnership is the deliberate design of how people and machines
share work at the task level. Rather than asking which jobs AI replaces, it
asks which tasks move to the machine, which stay human, and what that
reassignment does to roles, spans, decision rights and the operating model.

### What does an organization design strategist do?

An organization design strategist aligns an organization's structure and
accountabilities, people and skills, process and systems, and mindset and
behaviors so it can execute its strategy. The work spans diagnosis, operating
model design, and the change activation needed to make a new design real.

### How does AI change organization design?

AI redesigns the work, not the chart. The unit of analysis descends from the
org chart to the task, each task is placed on a ladder from manual to
reinvention, and any machine judgement is gated by a human before it reaches a
decision-maker. Structure follows work — and the work is now shared with
machines.

### What is Eric Yim’s background?

Eric Yim graduated from Nanyang Technological University in 1998 with a
Bachelor of Business specializing in financial analysis, and began his career
in corporate banking at Mizuho. He moved into organizational development
through the Civil Service College, then held organization development and
effectiveness roles at L’Oréal, Shell and Cargill before becoming Global Head
of OD and Talent at SATS Ltd.

### Where does Eric Yim work?

Eric Yim is Global Head of OD and Talent at SATS Ltd. in Singapore, which he
joined in December 2024. He previously spent over nine years at Shell in
global and regional organizational development leadership roles, and four
years at Cargill in organization effectiveness consulting.

### Why does Eric Yim say AI is a multiplier and not a shortcut?

Because a multiplier amplifies whatever expertise already exists — and zero
multiplied by any number is still zero. AI is most valuable to people with deep
domain expertise to amplify, not to those merely quickest to adopt the tools.
The discipline is discerning the right time and place to use AI.

### What principles guide Eric Yim’s work?

Eric Yim works from six principles: a system, not a report; one system, not
four fixes; not every difference is a problem; change is a behaviour, not an
announcement; AI redesigns the work, not the chart; and say what you know, and
how you know it. Each one is put to work in a part of his organizational
design playbook.

### How does Eric Yim approach an organization design engagement?

In six stages. Frame agrees how the design will be judged before anyone argues
for one. Focus finds where capability is weak where the value is made. Find
maps how the work really runs and who really decides. Dial decides what should
be one way everywhere and how much AI should do. Design scores structure, role
and system options against the criteria agreed at the start. Deliver tracks,
cycle by cycle, whether capability is actually lifting.

### What are required, chosen and inherited differences?

They are the three reasons the same work ends up done differently across
markets, sites or acquired units, and each calls for a different response. A
required difference is imposed by regulation, a customer contract or the
physical site, so it stays local. A chosen difference was a deliberate local
decision, so leaders decide whether to keep it or align it. An inherited
difference came from history, an acquisition or habit and nobody decided it,
so it should be harmonised. Two questions sort any difference: is it required,
and was it decided on purpose?

## Framework published on this site

The Integrated Organizational Capability and Change Framework: four
interdependent domains — Structure & Accountabilities, People & Skills,
Process & Systems, Mindset & Behaviors — around a Leadership core, inside a
ring of culture values. Supporting models: five activators that turn design
into performance; a three-lever change model (Communicate, Co-create,
Cadence); an AI-native design section (task-level descent, an L0–L3 automation
ladder, and human gating of machine judgement); and an 18-question diagnostic
scored across five dimensions.
